claims.text: The extent of atomic diffusion during cooling governs whether noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles form a uniform single-phase solid solution.
Controlled deceleration of cooling can provide an optimal kinetic window that balances atomic intermixing against kinetic trapping.
Cooling too rapidly causes kinetic trapping and compositional inhomogeneity.
Cooling too slowly permits excessive diffusion that causes elemental segregation and phase separation.
Rapid heating followed by rapid cooling often produces phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled particle morphology in these nanoparticles.
The cooling thermal profile determines the time available for atomic diffusion.
Rapid cooling kinetically traps atoms in an inhomogeneous or metastable state.
At an optimal slower cooling rate, diffusion allows atoms to overcome local energetic barriers and form a thermodynamically favored uniform single phase.
Relative to rapid quenching, controlled decelerated cooling will improve elemental homogeneity.
Relative to rapid quenching, controlled decelerated cooling will enhance crystallinity.
Relative to rapid quenching, controlled decelerated cooling will improve control of particle morphology.
Cooling rates outside the optimal window will increase phase separation or elemental segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble metal–based nanoparticles containing more than five elements with comparable atomic sizes and marginal mixing enthalpies.
Large elemental differences or processing conditions outside the diffusion-sensitive regime may prevent cooling-controlled diffusion from determining the phase outcome.
